notes.meaning: Korah was a Levite and a cousin of Moses. He led the revolt and drew in three men from the tribe of Reuben: Dathan, Abiram and On. Together they won over 250 well-known leaders of Israel. Korah may have been bitter that a man from a younger family line was made chief of his clan. The Reubenites may have resented losing the special rights of the firstborn. On is never mentioned again, so he may have backed out.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think two older stories were woven together here. One is about the Reubenites' revolt against Moses, and the other is about Korah's claim to the priesthood.

notes.meaning: The rebels accused Moses and Aaron of grabbing too much power. They said everyone in Israel was "holy," meaning set apart for God, so anyone could serve as priest. But God himself had chosen Moses and Aaron. The people had also sinned again and again, so they had little reason to boast. The rebels used a true idea to hide their own pride and ambition.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic writers link this verse with Jude 11, which warns against "Korah's rebellion" among Christians. They argue that this points to a special priesthood in the church, beyond the priesthood of all believers.

notes.meaning: Moses did not fight back or shout. He fell on his face before God in humble prayer. He asked God what to say and do before he answered the rebels. His trust in God mattered more than any show of strength.

Moses left the decision to God. In the morning, God would show whom he had chosen to come near him as priest. Waiting until the next day also gave the rebels a night to think again and turn back. Paul may echo this verse when he writes, "The Lord knows those who are his" (2 Timothy 2:19).

A censer was a small pan for carrying hot coals and incense. Burning incense was the holiest job a priest did. Not long before, Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu had died for offering it the wrong way. So this was a serious test. Moses then turned their own words back on them: "You have taken too much upon yourselves!"

Moses reminded Korah and the other Levites how much God had already given them. God had set them apart to serve at his tabernacle, his holy tent, and to help the people. That was a great honor. Yet they were not content and wanted the priesthood too. Thinking about how much we have already been given can help keep us from envying others.

Moses showed what was really going on. By fighting the leader God had chosen, they were fighting God himself. Aaron had not taken the priesthood for himself. God had called him to it, and he was only a servant doing what he was told.

Dathan and Abiram refused to come when Moses called them. That showed they did not accept his authority at all. They twisted the facts and called Egypt "a land flowing with milk and honey." They blamed Moses for not bringing them into Canaan, though it was the people's own unbelief that had kept them out. "Gouge out the eyes" means something like, "Do you think you can blind us and lead us around however you like?"

Moses was the humblest of men, but he grew very angry. His anger came mostly from zeal for God's honor. He asked God not to accept their offering, much as God had not accepted Cain's. He declared he had never taken even one donkey from them or harmed any of them. Unlike a greedy ruler, he had taken no payment for all his work.

Moses repeated the challenge. Korah and all 250 men were to bring censers with incense, and Aaron would bring one too. "Before the LORD" here means at the doorway of the tabernacle, where all the people could watch. Moses let Aaron stand on the same footing as his accusers, so the test would be fair and God alone would decide.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think these verses repeat verses 6-7 and were added when the story was put together.

notes.meaning: The rebels boldly came with their censers, even though they knew what had happened to Nadab and Abihu. Korah gathered a crowd to watch what he expected would be his win, and many people seemed to be on his side. Then God's glory appeared. Just as it had when Aaron first became priest, it now came to confirm him in that role.

God told Moses and Aaron to step away so he could destroy the crowd at once. By gathering with the rebels, the people had joined their cause. God was showing how serious their sin was and what it deserved.

Moses and Aaron fell on their faces and prayed for the very people who had turned against them. They called God "the God of the spirits of all flesh," meaning the Maker of every human life. He knows every heart and can tell the ringleader from those who were simply led astray. Like Abraham praying for Sodom, they asked God not to punish everyone for one man's sin. That one man was Korah.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the phrase "God of the spirits of all flesh" also appears in later Jewish writings. They think it may have been added later.

notes.meaning: God answered their prayer and agreed to spare the people. But they had to move away from the tents of Korah, Dathan and Abiram. By leaving, they would show they were turning from the rebels. Those who want to escape judgment must separate themselves from sin.

Dathan and Abiram had refused to come to Moses, so Moses humbly went to them. He was still trying to reach them. The seventy elders of Israel went with him. They showed their support for the leader God had chosen.
